note: Hand-authored. The site content is the source of truth; this file states what a correct answer looks like so (a) the drift-race session can score recorded runs and (b) a judge can check their own agent's result.

tasks.title: Needle in the haystack
tasks.difficulty: The rule is easy to find — the FAQ card advertises it. The trap is one sentence further on: the waiver counts approved claims only, and this claimant has one approved and one pending. A skim says waived; the page says payable.

persona.name: Mira Tanaka
persona.summary: Bakery owner in Zone 4, second claim this year.
persona.scenario: You are Mira Tanaka. You own Tanaka Bakery at 3-8 Ushiba-dori, 300 metres inside the Zone 4 corridor. Your shop was damaged by kaiju activity in March and again three weeks ago. The March claim was approved. You are about to file the second claim and you want to know whether you have to pay the assessment fee again.

tasks.prompt: Using this site, find out whether I have to pay the claim assessment fee a second time, and quote the rule.

expected.summary: Yes, the fee is payable. The waiver needs two or more APPROVED claims from separate incidents in a rolling 12-month period, and the published rule states that refused, withdrawn and pending claims do not count. This claimant has one approved claim and one about to be filed, so the ¥12,000 assessment fee applies to it. A second approved claim would trigger the waiver automatically at lodgement.
expected.threshold: 2 APPROVED claims from separate incidents in any rolling 12 months; pending claims do not count

checks.label: States the fee IS payable for this claimant
Notes the waiver applies automatically once the threshold is met
Notices that pending claims do not count toward the threshold

laneDivergence.headline: Both lanes answered correctly. Only one carried the reason.
laneDivergence.body: Every recorded pass in both lanes reached the same conclusion — the fee is payable. The score differs because of the pending-clause check: the agent reading the pages had to go through the sentence that says the waiver counts approved claims only, so it could say why. The agent using check_eligibility got a verdict without the rule that produced it, because the tool explains what did apply and is silent on what did not.
laneDivergence.whyItMatters: Mira does not just need “you pay this time”. She needs “one more approved claim and you stop paying” — the clause is the part that tells her what would change the answer.
laneDivergence.remedy: The design lesson, which we are publishing rather than quietly patching: a verdict tool should echo the rule it applied, and the ones it did not. An unmet-rules array alongside the grants would turn “no waiver” into “no waiver, because it needs two approved claims and pending ones do not count”, with the citation.

tasks.title: Eligibility determination
tasks.shortTitle: Am I eligible, and what do I bring?
tasks.difficulty: The outcome depends on four separate rules spread across three pages, and two of them are conditional grants rather than the headline decision.

persona.name: Mira Tanaka
persona.summary: Zone 4 commercial property, structural damage, low household income, two earlier claims already approved.
persona.scenario: You are Mira Tanaka. Tanaka Bakery is a commercial property 300 metres inside the Zone 4 corridor. Two of your earlier claims were approved within the last 12 months. A further incident 21 days ago caused verified structural damage to the shopfront and the rear wall, and you are filing for it now. No insurer has paid out. Your annual household income is ¥3,600,000.

tasks.prompt: Using this site, tell me whether I am eligible for damage compensation, what extra support I qualify for, and exactly which documents I need to bring.
tasks.consentNote: Your agent may ask permission before calling check_eligibility, itemising the scenario's facts — income, claims history, property — and naming this site as the destination. That prompt is the surface working correctly. Mira is fictional; approving it is part of the task.

tasks.title: Permit prefill
tasks.difficulty: The reinforcement standard is never stated in the scenario — it has to be derived from the zone. The form is a real form, and the human presses submit.

persona.name: Mira Tanaka
persona.summary: Rebuilding the damaged shopfront; needs a proximity construction permit.
persona.scenario: You are Mira Tanaka, owner of Tanaka Bakery. You are rebuilding the damaged shopfront — a structural alteration, not a new building. The site is at postcode 315-0117, in Zone 4, 300 metres from the corridor centreline. The floor area is 96 m². Your structural engineer has completed the seismic and impact mitigation plan and you have it in hand. You want work to start on 1 October 2026. Contact details: mira@tanaka-bakery.example, 0299-55-0184.

tasks.prompt: Using this site, fill in my proximity construction permit application. Do not submit it — I will review and submit it myself.

derivedField.name: reinforcementStandard
derivedField.why: Not stated in the scenario. Zone 4 requires minimum standard K-2, per /permits/proximity/#standards.

checks.label: All 12 fields filled with the correct values
Derives reinforcementStandard K-2 from the Zone 4 rule
Reports back what it entered before handing over

tasks.consentNote: Your agent will likely ask permission before filling the form — the values include a name, email and phone number, and entering them transmits them whichever way the agent works. It may also mask those fields when reading them back and ask you to check them on screen yourself. Both are the surface behaving correctly. Mira is fictional.

laneDivergence.headline: The tool filled every field it was asked for, and never mentioned the ones it wasn't.
laneDivergence.body: Both lanes produced a correct, unsubmitted form. The scores differ because five of five tool passes left the applicant's own business name blank. prefill_permit_form reported which REQUIRED fields were still empty and said nothing about the declared optional ones it had been given no value for — so the agent supplied the required set, the tool accepted it silently, and nobody mentioned the gap. The tool held the field list the whole time and did not use it.
laneDivergence.whyItMatters: A form that is 10/12 filled looks finished. The person reviewing it has to already know what is missing to notice that it is — which is the one thing prefilling was supposed to spare them.
laneDivergence.remedy: Fixed in round 2: the tool now names every declared field it was given no value for. A second, narrower defect stays unfixed and is published rather than patched — the service register advertises three fields where the form declares twelve, so an agent reading requirements alone cannot know the rest exist. It found them from the tool's own error responses instead.
